```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = TRUE,
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 110
)
options(width = 85)
# Helpers for numbers quoted in the text (nothing below is typed in by hand).
quoted <- function(x) {
  x <- paste0("\u201c", x, "\u201d")
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    x
  } else {
    paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
  }
}
num <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  ifelse(
    is.finite(x),
    formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f", big.mark = ","),
    "not estimated"
  )
}
count <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
one_line <- function(x) gsub("\\s*\n\\s*", " ", as.character(x))
```

This tutorial shows how to explore whether the effect of one variable on another is larger for some people than for others. You need three things:

- a **dependent variable (Y)**, the variable you want to explain: binary, with any two values (such as voted or did not vote), or continuous (such as a test score);
- an **independent variable (W)**, whose effect on Y you want to study: binary, with any two values (such as treated or untreated), or continuous (such as hours of use) (see [5. Other analyses](#5-other-analyses));
- **characteristics (X)** that might moderate the effect, that is, make it larger or smaller.

A causal forest estimates the effect of W for people with different characteristics and points to patterns worth investigating.

The example uses the 2024 General Social Survey (GSS). Y is a rating of Donald Trump from 0 to 100. W compares respondents who identify as conservative with those who identify as liberal or moderate. Political identification was not randomly assigned, so we read the results as **adjusted associations**, not causal effects.

The package can be used in two ways: with its R functions, as in this tutorial, or as a local app that does the same on one page without code (see [6. The app](#6-the-app)). The tutorial has four steps: choose variables, run the forest, look at the treatment effect by candidate moderator, and export the results. Sections 5 and 6 cover other analyses and the app.

## 1. Choose variables

Install the package as described in the [README](../README.md#installation). Then load the package and the example, which ships with it:

```{r load}
library(heterogeneity)
gss <- load_gss2024()
```

`load_gss2024()` reads an extract of NORC's complete 2024 release, prepared with every recode checked against the GSS category labels. `gss$data` has one row for each of the `r count(nrow(gss$data))` respondents with a value for both Y and W. `gss$covariates` names `r length(gss$covariates)` demographic, socioeconomic, religious, attitudinal and wellbeing characteristics, and `gss$codebook` describes every column, with its role, GSS source item and notes. The file also holds further dependent and independent variables for other analyses, such as ratings of Kamala Harris and of the two parties, and a college degree:

```{r codebook, eval=FALSE}
gss$codebook[
  gss$codebook$variable %in%
    c("rating_trump", "conservative", "age", "lkelyvot"),
  c("variable", "label", "coding")
]
```

```{r codebook-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  gss$codebook[
    gss$codebook$variable %in%
      c("rating_trump", "conservative", "age", "lkelyvot"),
    c("variable", "label", "coding")
  ],
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

The notes matter for some characteristics: for example, the likelihood of voting was not asked of respondents who were not U.S. citizens, so they are missing on it.

```{r missing-numbers, include=FALSE}
share_missing <- colMeans(is.na(gss$data[gss$covariates]))
most_missing <- names(which.max(share_missing))
```

Choose characteristics that make sense for your question. If you want to read the results causally, use only characteristics that W could not have changed.

**How the data are prepared.** `explore_heterogeneity()` tidies the data before fitting, and the report's notes list every change:

- blank cells, infinite numbers and common missing-value text ("NA", "N/A", "NaN", "NULL", ".", "-") count as missing, and text columns that hold only numbers are read as numbers;
- rows missing Y or W (or a supplied weight or cluster) are left out of the analysis;
- characteristics that are entirely missing or constant are left out;
- text characteristics (up to 20 categories) become 0/1 indicators, one per category, so any category can be split off; their importance is added back up afterwards;
- numbers are treated as ordered values, so turn unordered codes (such as region codes) into text first;
- the notes also flag characteristics with more than half of their values missing, pairs of characteristics correlated at |r| ≥ 0.9 (which share importance), and groups of W with fewer than 10 rows (whose estimates are very noisy).

**Keep missing characteristics.** The forest handles missing values directly, so nothing needs to be filled in. Here the characteristic missing most often is `r quoted(gss$labels[[most_missing]])`, for `r num(100 * share_missing[[most_missing]])`% of respondents. This avoids inventing values, but it does not remove bias when values are missing for systematic reasons. Rows missing Y or W (or a supplied weight or cluster) are left out, and the report lists every such change.

## 2. Run the forest

One call fits the forest, and printing the report shows a summary and draws two plots. The labels are optional; here they come from the example.

```{r report, fig.keep="none"}
report <- explore_heterogeneity(
  data = gss$data,
  y = "rating_trump",
  w = "conservative",
  x = gss$covariates,
  ids = "id",
  labels = gss$labels,
  value_labels = gss$value_labels,
  effect_label = gss$effect_label
)
report
```

```{r report-numbers, include=FALSE}
groups <- report$settings$w_labels
direction <- if (report$ate$estimate >= 0) "higher" else "lower"
below <- mean(report$estimates < 0)
below_text <- if (below == 0) {
  "every estimated treatment effect is above 0"
} else if (below == 1) {
  "every estimated treatment effect is below 0"
} else {
  sprintf(
    "%s%% of the estimated treatment effects are below 0",
    num(100 * below, 0)
  )
}
rows <- c(importance = nrow(report$moderators))
```

**The summary.** The average treatment effect is **`r num(report$ate$estimate)` rating points**: on average, `r tolower(groups[2])` respondents rate Trump `r num(abs(report$ate$estimate))` points `r direction` than `r tolower(groups[1])` respondents with similar characteristics. "Treatment effect" is the standard name for this quantity; because W was not randomly assigned here, it is an adjusted association rather than a causal effect. It also differs from simply subtracting the two group means, because it compares people with similar characteristics.

In standard deviations the average is **`r num(report$ate$standardized, 2)`**: the difference divided by how much ratings vary within the two groups, before adjustment (one standard deviation is `r num(report$ate$sd_y)` points). This standardized effect size can be compared across dependent variables measured in different units. Everything else stays in rating points; dividing by `report$ate$sd_y` converts any of it.

The forest also estimates a treatment effect for each combination of characteristics (a conditional average treatment effect, CATE); these range from `r num(report$prediction_range[1])` to `r num(report$prediction_range[2])` points. They come from `r count(report$settings$num_trees)` honest trees: each tree uses one part of the data to choose its splits and another part to estimate the effects, and each respondent's estimate comes only from trees grown without them ("out-of-bag"). Every average in this tutorial, overall, in a group or along a characteristic, uses doubly robust scores, which combine the estimates with the observed ratings; grf recommends this over averaging the estimates themselves. The candidate moderators are the characteristics the forest used most in its splits, and the data notes list everything that was changed or left out.

Below, the two plots are shown one at a time, each with its explanation. `plot(report)` and `plot(report, "importance")` draw them on their own, for example to save one.

```{r plot-1}
plot(report)
```

**Plot 1: distribution of estimated treatment effects, conditional on covariates.** The histogram shows each respondent's estimated treatment effect, with the number of bins chosen from the data (the Freedman–Diaconis rule). The colours deepen with distance from 0, which the dashed line marks, and the solid line marks the average treatment effect, with its value. Teal bars, above 0, are estimates in which `r tolower(groups[2])` respondents rate Trump higher than `r tolower(groups[1])` respondents with similar characteristics, and the further above 0, the deeper the teal; red bars, below 0, would show the reverse. Here `r below_text`. These are model estimates: part of their spread is estimation noise, so the plot is not the true distribution of individual effects, and the lowest and highest estimates are the least reliable.

```{r plot-2, fig.height = 1.2 + 0.2 * rows[["importance"]]}
plot(report, "importance")
```

**Plot 2: candidate moderators of the treatment effect, ranked by importance.** The chart ranks all `r rows[["importance"]]` characteristics. The top-ranked one is **`r report$moderators$label[1]`**. Importance measures how often, and how early, the forest split on a characteristic. That makes it a candidate moderator, not a proven one: importance does not say whether the treatment effect rises or falls with the characteristic, and related characteristics share importance. For a text characteristic, the importance of its indicators is added together.

A few options are worth knowing:

- `W_hat`: in a randomized experiment, the known probability of being in the group coded 1, such as `W_hat = 0.5`; otherwise, as here, the forest estimates it.
- `treated` and `y_one`: for a binary W or Y, the value coded 1; by default the larger (or alphabetically later) value, so effects are that value minus the other.
- `weights` and `clusters`: survey weights apply to the forest and to every average; clusters, such as students in the same school, are sampled together, while each observation still counts once in averages. Here `weights = "svy_weight"` would describe U.S. adults. This illustration is unweighted, so it describes these respondents, who include an oversample of Black, Hispanic, and Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander respondents.
- `controls`: characteristics to adjust for but not to study as moderators, such as common causes of W and Y. The forest uses them like every other characteristic, so each estimated treatment effect accounts for them, but the importance ranking and the plots leave them out.
- `seed`: the default (`r format(report$settings$seed, scientific = FALSE)`) makes the results reproducible.

`print(report, plots = FALSE)` shows the summary without the plots, and with many characteristics `top_n` limits the importance plot, for example `plot(report, "importance", top_n = 10)`.

## 3. Treatment effect by candidate moderator

`effect_by()` shows how the treatment effect varies with one characteristic: it estimates the average treatment effect within the characteristic's groups, and `plot()` draws the result. The app shows this plot for every candidate moderator, in order of importance; in R, `for (v in report$moderators$variable) print(plot(effect_by(report, v)))` does the same. We start with likelihood of voting, which ranks `r which(report$moderators$variable == "lkelyvot")` of `r nrow(report$moderators)` in importance.

```{r voting-table}
voting <- effect_by(report, "lkelyvot")
voting
```

```{r voting-numbers, include=FALSE}
observed <- voting[voting$lkelyvot != "(Missing)", ]
lowest <- observed[1, ]
highest <- observed[nrow(observed), ]
category <- function(code) {
  tolower(gss$value_labels$lkelyvot[[as.character(code)]])
}
```

Each row is a group of respondents, labelled by its code (the codebook above gives the meaning). `n_control` counts the `r tolower(groups[1])` respondents in the group and `n_treated` the `r tolower(groups[2])` ones. A group with fewer than 10 respondents, or with only one group of W, gets no estimate, and its `status` says why. The average treatment effect is `r num(lowest$estimate)` points among respondents who are `r category(lowest$lkelyvot)` to vote and `r num(highest$estimate)` among those who are `r category(highest$lkelyvot)`. The table includes respondents with a missing answer as a group of their own; the plot leaves them out. The plot shows each respondent's estimated treatment effect, with a line for the average treatment effect across the five categories. With so few values the line is smoothed widely, so it shows the trend rather than each category's own average, which the table gives. Its y axis is the treatment effect, a dashed line marks 0, and the caption gives the overall average treatment effect:

```{r voting-plot}
plot(voting)
```

These groups also differ in other ways, so the plot does not show what would happen if someone's likelihood of voting changed. Check characteristics your theory names as well as the top-ranked ones:

```{r age-plot}
age <- effect_by(report, "age")
plot(age)
```

```{r age-numbers, include=FALSE}
age_observed <- age[age$age != "(Missing)", ]
first_age <- age_observed[1, ]
last_age <- age_observed[nrow(age_observed), ]
line <- attr(age, "plot")$smooth
line_low <- line[which.min(line$effect), ]
line_high <- line[which.max(line$effect), ]
# The same loess through the estimates themselves, to compare how far each
# rises and falls.
rows_age <- attr(age, "plot")$rows
points_line <- stats::predict(
  stats::loess(effect ~ value, data = rows_age),
  data.frame(value = line$value)
)
steeper <- diff(range(line$effect)) > diff(range(points_line))
```

For a numeric characteristic such as age, each point is one respondent's estimated treatment effect, and the line is the average treatment effect along age: a loess smooth (the line `geom_smooth(method = "loess")` would draw) of the same doubly robust scores behind every average. The line is lowest near age `r round(line_low$value)` (about `r num(line_low$effect)` points) and highest near age `r round(line_high$value)` (about `r num(line_high$effect)` points). The table `age` gives the average treatment effect in up to five age groups of about equal size: `r num(first_age$estimate)` points for ages `r as.character(first_age$age)` and `r num(last_age$estimate)` for ages `r as.character(last_age$age)`.`r if (steeper) " The line rises and falls more than the points do, because each estimated treatment effect is pulled toward the overall average." else ""` Both describe people of different ages, not the effect of growing older, and the group boundaries are not thresholds.

A text characteristic, such as region, has no order, so its plot shows the average treatment effect in each group as a point instead of a line.

**How the averages are computed.** Every average in these plots and tables, like the overall average treatment effect, comes from grf's doubly robust scores rather than from the estimated treatment effects themselves, which are pulled toward the overall average; a group's average equals grf's own estimate for that group. The package does not form groups from the estimated treatment effects (such as their top and bottom fifths), because grf warns that such groups give misleading averages unless a separate sample is used to evaluate them.

Two characteristics give a heatmap (in the app, choose a second characteristic above any plot):

```{r two-way, fig.height=6}
two <- effect_by(report, "lkelyvot", "income16")
plot(two)
```

```{r two-way-numbers, include=FALSE}
income_sizes <- tapply(two$n, two$income16, sum)
income_sizes <- income_sizes[names(income_sizes) != "(Missing)"]
```

With two characteristics, numeric ones with more than eight values are cut into three groups of about equal size, each characteristic on its own, at its own thirds. Tied values stay in one group, so the groups can be unequal: income, recorded in `r length(unique(stats::na.omit(gss$data$income16)))` ordered categories rather than dollar amounts, splits into `r paste(sprintf("%s (%s respondents)", names(income_sizes), count(income_sizes)), collapse = ", ")`. Each cell shows an average treatment effect and its number of respondents, coloured around the overall average treatment effect, as the legend's "Treatment effect" scale shows. A cell with too few respondents, or with only one group of W, is not estimated and appears grey. The heatmap leaves out respondents missing either characteristic; the table from `effect_by(report, "lkelyvot", "income16")` includes them.

## 4. Export results

Save each respondent's estimated treatment effect, the group estimates and the importance ranking as ordinary CSV files:

```{r export, eval=FALSE}
write.csv(report$cates, "treatment_effects.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(effect_by(report, "age"), "age_groups.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(report$moderators, "importance.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

`report$cates` has one row per row of `gss$data`, in the same order: the row number, the respondent's `id` and the estimated treatment effect, which is empty for any row that was not analysed (`r if (report$n_dropped == 0) "here, every respondent was analysed" else paste(count(report$n_dropped), "rows here")`). It can therefore be put next to the data directly.

A short report can say:

> Among `r count(report$settings$n)` GSS respondents, those identifying as conservative rated Trump `r num(abs(report$ate$estimate))` points (`r num(abs(report$ate$standardized), 2)` standard deviations) `r direction`, on average, than liberal or moderate respondents with similar characteristics. The characteristics the forest used most were `r quoted(report$moderators$label[1:3])`. Across voting-likelihood groups, the average treatment effect ranged from `r num(min(observed$estimate, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r num(max(observed$estimate, na.rm = TRUE))` points. The analysis was unweighted, and missing characteristics were kept for the forest rather than filled in. These patterns are exploratory: estimated treatment effects describe people with similar characteristics and include noise.

Add the group estimates and counts relevant to your question. A causal reading needs a defensible research design, comparable groups and suitable characteristics; the GSS example makes no causal claim.

## 5. Other analyses

The example file also holds further dependent variables (ratings of Kamala Harris, Joe Biden, the two parties and MAGA Republicans, the rating of the economy and the preferred immigration level) and a further independent variable (a college degree); `gss$codebook` lists each column's role. The same functions handle controls, a binary Y and a continuous W:

```{r other, eval=FALSE}
# Controls: adjust for sex and age without studying them as moderators.
adjusted <- explore_heterogeneity(
  data = gss$data,
  y = "rating_trump",
  w = "conservative",
  x = setdiff(gss$covariates, c("female", "age")),
  controls = c("female", "age")
)
# A binary Y: effects are differences in the share coded 1
# (here, being married).
married <- explore_heterogeneity(
  data = gss$data,
  y = "married",
  w = "college",
  x = setdiff(gss$covariates, c("married", "degree", "educ"))
)
# A continuous W: effects are slopes, the change in Y per one-unit
# increase in W.
slopes <- explore_heterogeneity(
  data = gss$data,
  y = "rating_trump",
  w = "educ",
  x = setdiff(gss$covariates, c("educ", "degree"))
)
```

With controls, the printed summary counts them separately ("`r length(gss$covariates) - 2` candidate moderators and 2 controls"), and they appear in neither the importance ranking nor `effect_by()`, just like the app's Controls field. Leave out of X any characteristic that measures the same thing as Y or W, as degree and years of education do for a college degree. For a continuous W, grf estimates a local slope for each combination of characteristics and averages them into the average partial effect; a group in `effect_by()` gets an estimate only when W varies within it.

## 6. The app

`heterogeneity::run_app()` opens the same analysis as a local app in your browser, without code. Upload a CSV, TSV, Excel, SPSS (.sav) or Stata (.dta) file, or load the GSS example. The app finds the delimiter and text encoding of text files, recognises a missing header row and uses SPSS and Stata labels as readable names. It shows the first 10 rows, then every field at once: Y, W, candidate moderators, optional controls, and default parameters (an ID column, weights, clusters, the number of trees and the seed). **Select all** chooses the remaining columns as candidate moderators.

**Run the causal forest** shows all results on one page once they are ready: the average treatment effect, the two plots of step 2, a plot for each candidate moderator in order of importance (each with an optional second characteristic for a heatmap), and the export, a file with one row per row of your data in the same order. Hovering over an underlined term explains it, and changing any input clears the results until you run the forest again. The app runs in your own R session; uploaded files are not stored and are deleted when the session ends.

The [grf guide](https://grf-labs.github.io/grf/articles/grf_guide.html) explains the underlying method and its handling of missing values.

```{r versions, echo=FALSE}
    vapply(

)
```
